Just now

--

Two weeks into global design workshops to rebuild the foundation of Workday for a large organization, I keep coming back to the same question. It has nothing to do with Workday itself and everything to do with why we design enterprise HR platforms the way we do.
Shift One: The Business Process Has a User Problem
Every Workday business process assumes a human at a screen. The documentation says “manager initiates the process.” In these workshops, that sentence rarely survives the discussion.
Someone always asks: do we actually want managers logging into Workday for this at all?
What if a manager simply told an AI assistant: “Promote Sarah to Senior Manager effective next month.” “Open a requisition for a Software Engineer in Barcelona.” “Approve John’s vacation.” The AI understands the request, checks policy, asks a clarifying question if it needs to, executes the right business process underneath, and confirms. The manager never opens Workday.
This wasn’t a one-off idea in a single session. It became a recurring design principle. The conversation quietly moved from how users should navigate the system to how AI should act on the system on their behalf. The manager isn’t the user of Workday anymore. They’re the user of a conversational layer that happens to call Workday.
The system of record is becoming invisible infrastructure, not a destination.
Shift Two: If Nobody’s Logging In, What Are We Paying For?
Once you see that shift, a harder question follows. If managers and employees are meant to interact through an AI layer rather than the platform’s native UI, what exactly are we paying a premium enterprise SaaS multiple for?
A large part of what you buy with a platform like Workday is the front end: self-service screens, configurable workflows, mobile experiences. If that layer is being routed around in favor of a conversational AI experience, the case for paying for it changes. A leaner model, a well-governed structural data layer serving as the single source of truth for jobs, org, comp, and worker data, paired with an AI interface the company builds and owns on top of it, is a real alternative architecture. I think it deserves to be evaluated as one, not dismissed as a shortcut. Most vendor conversations, and most internal governance conversations I sit in, aren’t asking this question yet. They should be.

Workday Is Already Repositioning Around This
Workday hasn’t missed this.
Its strategy around AI agents, the Agent System of Record, Sana, developer tooling, and governed agent access all point toward the same future: people increasingly interact through AI, while Workday provides trusted data, governance, orchestration, and execution behind the scenes. Workday has even begun talking about Agent Experience (AX) alongside User Experience (UX), acknowledging that enterprise software increasingly needs to be designed for both humans and AI agents.
I don’t read that as proof Workday has settled the question in its own favor. I read it as validation of the premise. Even the vendor whose pricing model depends on the self-service interface is telling customers the interface isn’t where the value is anymore. That doesn’t answer whether the rest of the bundle, at that price, from that vendor, is still the right architecture. It sharpens the question.
The real decision in front of large organizations isn’t keep the platform or replace it with a database. It’s whose governance and orchestration layer sits under your AI experience: the vendor’s, or one you control. Most companies are defaulting to the vendor’s answer without ever treating it as a decision.
What I’m Not Arguing
A platform like Workday isn’t only a UI. It’s a maintained data model, a compliance and localization engine across dozens of countries, a security and audit framework, and a vendor that carries the burden of keeping payroll and tax logic current as regulations shift. Any leaner alternative has to replicate a meaningful part of that: real cost, real engineering, not a shortcut. This isn’t a call to rip and replace.
The Reframe I’m Working With
For the last twenty years, HR technology optimized for one thing: making systems easier for people to use themselves. Adoption meant getting people to log in and use the tool well. We invested millions making self-service better.
That assumption is breaking, and most organizations haven’t caught up. The strategic investment is no longer the system and its self-service configuration. It’s the AI-mediated journey itself: how a manager experiences asking for something in natural language and getting it handled correctly, safely, and compliantly, regardless of which system executes it underneath. The money and design attention should be moving away from which platform has the best configurable workflows and toward which data foundation is clean enough to be a trustworthy source for AI, and how good the journey is that we build on top of it.
If you’re sitting in similar design rooms right now: is your organization actually treating who owns the AI orchestration layer as a decision, or defaulting to the vendor by habit?
